articles.title: Delhi court issues non-bailable warrant against Dhruv Rathee in 2018 defamation case
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A Delhi court on Monday (November 23, 2026) issued a non-bailable warrant (NBW) against YouTuber Dhruv Rathee in a 2018 defamation case.
Judicial Magistrate Anam Rais Khan issued the warrant in a case filed by Vikas Sanskrityayan alias Vikas Pandey over a video uploaded on Mr. Rathee's YouTube channel.
The matter has been posted for further proceedings on December 3. A detailed order is awaited.
Earlier on October 31, the court had issued fresh bailable warrants against Mr. Rathee.

On October 17, it had issued bailable warrants against him after a process server reported that his house was locked while attempting to serve notice. The court had also issued fresh summons to Mr. Rathee at his address in Gurugram, Haryana.
His advocate had submitted that Mr. Rathee ordinarily resides in Austria and had come to India for the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protests in Delhi.
The court had noted that Mr. Rathee was initially summoned in July 2019.
The case pertains to a defamation complaint filed by Mr. Pandey in 2018 after Mr. Rathee uploaded a video against him on his YouTube channel.

articles.title: ASEAN-India Maritime Conclave in Visakhapatnam calls for deeper cooperation to secure Indo-Pacific trade routes
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Policymakers, diplomats and naval officials called for deeper regional cooperation to safeguard Indo-Pacific trade routes, address geopolitical uncertainties and build a resilient blue economy as the two-day ASEAN-India Maritime Conclave commenced on Monday (November 23, 2026) in Visakhapatnam .

Organised by the India Foundation in partnership with the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), the conclave brought together Union Minister of State for External Affairs Pabitra Margherita, Andhra Pradesh Minister for Human Resources Development, IT and Electronics Nara Lokesh, Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Krishna Swaminathan, former Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Dinesh Kumar Tripathi, India Foundation President Ram Madhav and ambassadors and strategic thinkers from ASEAN member states.

Addressing the inaugural session, Mr. Margherita said that ASEAN-India synergy was central to India’s Indo-Pacific vision and Act East Policy, adding that stronger maritime connectivity, disaster management and sustainable blue economy partnerships were vital as both sides marked the Year of ASEAN-India Maritime Cooperation.

Union Minister of State for External Affairs Pabitra Margherita (left), Vice Chief of the Naval Staff Vice Admiral Krishna Swaminathan (centre) and Andhra Pradesh Minister for Human Resources Development, IT and Electronics Nara Lokesh at the inaugural session of the two-day ASEAN-India Maritime Conclave in Visakhapatnam on Monday. | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

Admiral Swaminathan cautioned that geopolitical shifts, climate change, and extreme weather events were creating uncertainty across the Indo-Pacific’s 12 million square kilometres of exclusive economic zones, where security is tested daily by maritime terrorism, cyber threats, theft, and trespassing—challenges that require shared regional responsibility to ensure secure sea lanes.

Mr. Lokesh pitched Andhra Pradesh’s 1,053-km coastline—backed by four upcoming ports, a proposed ₹30,000-crore shipbuilding cluster at Dugarajapatnam, subsea cable landing infrastructure, and green ammonia exports—as an industrial and digital gateway for ASEAN supply chains.

Meanwhile, Mr. Madhav said that Visakhapatnam was among the country’s foremost maritime stations, adding that the conclave would deliberate on recent shipping disruptions and channel closures to revitalise Indo-Pacific commerce.

Over two days, delegates and maritime experts will discuss port modernisation, maritime domain awareness, coastal resilience and institutional frameworks to turn diplomatic convergence into regional partnerships.

articles.title: West Bengal to be renamed Paschim Banga
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A proposal to rename West Bengal as ‘Paschim Banga’ will be tabled in the State Assembly on December 9, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said on Monday (November 23, 2026).

“West Bengal will be known as ‘Paschim Banga’ in English as well. The name must be written exactly as ‘Paschim Banga’. We will introduce a resolution in the Assembly on the 9th. After its passage, it will be sent to the Government of India for the necessary parliamentary and legal procedures,” Mr. Adhikari said after a Cabinet meeting at the State Secretariat.
The State is referred to as ‘Paschim Banga’ in Bengali, and the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government wants the same name to be used in English.
“The formation of West Bengal has a history dating back to June 20, 1947, and that history must be recognised. Instead of ‘West Bengal’, the name will be ‘Paschim Banga’,” the Chief Minister said.

The BJP leadership in West Bengal has often emphasised that the word ‘Paschim Banga’ is part of the history of the creation of the State, which bore the brunt of Partition, and that one part of it became East Bengal [ Purba Bangla ], which is now Bangladesh. By using ‘Paschim Banga’, the BJP wants to highlight how Shyama Prasad Mookerjee and others sought the State as a homeland for ‘Bengali Hindus’ during Partition.
On June 20, the BJP government observed Paschimbanga Divas, marking the date in 1947 when Jana Sangha founder Mookerjee moved a proposal in the Bengal Legislative Assembly to partition Bengal.

The Trinamool Congress government had passed a resolution to rename West Bengal as ‘Bangla’ in July 2018, but the Union government did not consider Mamata Banerjee’ government’s repeated requests to change the State’s official name to ‘Bangla’.

articles.title: Calcutta High Court extends interim protection to TMC MP Abhishek Banerjee till February 26 in six criminal cases
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Calcutta High Court on Monday (November 23, 2026) extended interim protection from coercive action to TMC MP Abhishek Banerjee in six criminal cases lodged against him at various police stations in West Bengal.
Justice Saugata Bhattacharyya extended the protection in two separate petitions filed by Mr. Banerjee in connection with the six cases registered against him since May this year.
The interim protection granted to the Diamond Harbour MP will remain in force till February 26, 2027, or until further orders, whichever is earlier.

Hearing a petition seeking extension of the protection granted to him on August 25 in three of the cases , Justice Bhattacharyya noted that the investigations were yet to be completed and there had been no change in circumstances warranting denial of the extension sought by Mr. Banerjee.

Additional Advocate General Billwadal Bhattacharya, appearing for the state in connection with the three cases, submitted that a special leave petition (SLP) had been filed before the Supreme Court challenging the high court’s August 25 order and that it was pending consideration.
Seeking an extension of the interim protection, Mr. Banerjee’s counsel Gopal Sankaranarayan told the court that the SLP pending before the Supreme Court was a defective appeal.
The State had opposed Banerjee’s plea for extension of the interim protection granted by the High Court on August 25.
The protection from coercive action by police in these three cases relates to FIRs registered at Bhowanipore, Bishnupur and Kalitala police stations.

In connection with three other cases registered at Rabindranagar and Bishnupur police stations in South 24 Parganas district, the state submitted communications detailing the progress of investigations in two of them.
Mr. Sankaranarayan sought an extension of the interim protection granted to Banerjee on September 7 in connection with these three cases.
Additional Advocate General Rajdeep Majumdar, appearing for the state, opposed the plea.

Noting that investigations in the three cases were continuing, Justice Bhattacharyya extended the interim protection from coercive action till February 26, 2027, or until further orders, whichever is earlier.

articles.title: Lakshmi Aparna sworn in as Guntur Mayor; JSP’s Rajesh is Deputy Mayor
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Kovelamudi Lakshmi Aparna of the Telugu Desam Party (TDP) was sworn in as the new Mayor of the Guntur Municipal Corporation on Monday (November 23, 2026). Ward 64 corporator Yarramsetti Rajesh of the Jana Sena Party (JSP) was unanimously elected Deputy Mayor at the ceremony.
District Collector and Presiding Officer C.M. Saikanth Varma administered the oath of office to the Mayor and all 76 corporators, who attended the ceremony.

Subsequently, Mr. Rajesh was elected Deputy Mayor after his candidature was proposed by Ward 24 corporator Nimmala Venkata Ramana and seconded by Muthineni Rajesh and Irri Sai, corporators representing the 45th and 6th wards, respectively. Since there were no other candidates, the Presiding Officer declared him unanimously elected.

Addressing the gathering, Ms. Aparna said her priority was to ensure basic infrastructure for every household and make the civic body one of the best municipal corporations in the country. She promised to remain accessible to citizens and address their grievances through coordination between elected representatives and officials.
The Collector congratulated the newly elected representatives and assured the district administration’s full cooperation in the city’s development.

MLCs Alapati Rajendra Prasad and Chandragiri Yesuratnam, MLAs Nazeer Ahmed, Galla Madhavi and Burla Ramanjaneyulu, Jana Sena district president Gade Venkateswara Rao and Municipal Commissioner Mayur Ashok attended the ceremony.

articles.title: Nepal PM India visit LIVE: PM Modi announces offshore campus of IIT in Nepal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: “As a dependable and trusted neighbour, India consistently stood as the first responder in times of natural disasters and difficult times in Nepal,” Nepal PM Balen Shah said, adding that mutual respect, steadfast trust and unbroken goodwill are the bedrock of the relations.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while announcing the Development Cooperation Package of 24,000 crore Nepalese rupees, expressed his condolences over the loss of lives in the Nepal floods.

PM Modi announced that India will establish an offshore campus of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) in Nepal, alongside a startup incubator and an innovation hub, as part of a broader push to empower Nepali youth and deepen bilateral educational and technological cooperation.

“Friends, Nepal’s youth generation is full of talent, energy, and big dreams. India is fully committed to partnering in making their dreams a reality. To realise this resolve, we will establish a startup incubator, an innovation hub, and an offshore campus of the Indian Institute of Technology in Nepal,” PM Modi said.

Alongside setting up the IIT offshore campus, the Prime Minister announced expanded academic avenues in India for students from the Himalayan nation, stating, “We will expand scholarship opportunities in India for Nepali students in law and technology.”

Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a development package of 24,000 crore Nepalese rupees for Nepal after holding wide-ranging talks with his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah that produced many key outcomes to further solidify the bilateral ties.

Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah warmly welcomed Indian investors to Nepal and called for translating bilateral understandings and infrastructure milestones into tangible gains for farmers, youth, students, and entrepreneurs across both countries.

“We are clear that the outcomes of the understandings that we reached today, and the projects we advance, must translate into prosperity in the fields of our farmers, employment and opportunity in the hands of our youth, new horizons in the dreams of our students, and tangible avenues for new markets, investment, and business expansion for our entrepreneurs. I am confident that these historic milestones will elevate Nepal-India relations to new heights. The need of the hour is to stand on the sturdy foundation of this enduring bond,” he added.
India will establish an offshore campus of IIT, expand scholarship opportunities in Law and Technology for Nepali students in India, says PM Modi.
The Prime Minister underscored New Delhi’s role in keeping fuel, fertiliser, and other essentials flowing to Nepal under its “Neighbourhood First” approach despite supply pressures this year.

“In keeping with our ‘Neighbourhood First’ policy, despite severe challenges in oil supply this year, we maintained uninterrupted supplies of fuel, fertiliser, and other essential goods to Nepal. Today, the dedication of Phase II of the Motihari–Amlekhgunj pipeline and the foundation stone laying for the Jhapa petroleum terminal will further strengthen this partnership,” he stated.
The energy and fuel initiatives were unveiled alongside a Joint Vision Document aimed at advancing shared goals of “Viksit Bharat” and “Samunnat Nepal” he added.

articles.title: Core accountability: On core sector performance
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The core sector performance in October is a good example of how statistical distortions can create incorrect assessments of the economy. The 10.9% growth rate, a series high, has been celebrated as a sign of the Indian economy’s strength and resilience. There is, no doubt, an aspect of this has been reflected in the numbers, especially to do with infrastructure creation. However, the much more impactful factor behind the high core sector growth was a low base effect. The overall Index of Core Industries grew just 0.8% in October 2025 and so, in relation, the performance in October 2026 looked that much faster. This low base effect is even starker when looking at individual sectors within the index. The coal sector grew at a blistering 23% in October, more than twice its growth rate in the previous month. Yet, a large part of this was propelled by the fact that the sector had contracted nearly 8.5% last October. The rest of the sector’s growth was driven by demand of the electricity and iron ore sectors, or so the data show. The electricity sector also grew at a series high of nearly 22% in October, but on the back of a near-7% contraction in October last year. This base effect anomaly is likely down to the fact that the festive season starts at different but similar points every year. As such, a more accurate reading of the economy will be possible once the data for November are available.

The construction-related sectors seem to have seen genuine growth, a reflection of the government’s ongoing infrastructure push. The iron ore sector’s growth rate accelerated to a three-month high of 26.4% in October 2026 as compared to a growth of 8.7% in the same month last year. Steel grew at 7.3% versus 9.5% last year, and cement by 15.4% versus 5.2%. The economy’s dependence on government spending is not going to ease in the near future, and might even intensify as higher costs eat into companies’ profit margins. The core sector data once again highlighted a major reason for these higher costs — the oil and gas sectors. The crude oil sector shrank by 4.1%, its 22nd consecutive month of contraction. The natural gas sector, similarly, contracted 7.6%, a series-worst performance and the 28th straight month of contraction. A major reason behind high inflation in India is the underperformance of these two sectors and the resultant dependence on imported fuel. It is time the Petroleum Ministry candidly explains — to Parliament in December or to the public directly — why India’s fuel output has been continuously falling. If it is a matter of a lack of resources underground, that is one thing, but the underperformance of oil and gas public sector undertakings is quite another. Accountability needs to be set.

articles.title: Rampur’s Lavi Fair: Storytelling through 300 years of Himalayan trade and tradition
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: What Disneyland is to children today, Lavi Fair in Rampur Bushahr, in Himachal Pradesh’s Shimla district, was to my family in the 1980s. I recall wandering through the fair as an eight-year-old, watching an old man smoking a chillum beside heaps of black sheep fleece and stacks of white woollen pattus (traditional garments of Kinnaur and Kullu women).

Mother and her friends carefully chose shawls for their daughters’ and future daughters-in-law’s trousseaux. Years later, I received a beautiful black sheep wool and pashmina shawl for my wedding. Wool finds pride of place at the fair. The name Lavi is linked to “Loe”, a sheet of woollen cloth and the practice of shearing sheep.

articles.title: Must balance ‘economic patriotism’ with cultural heritage: GJC on PM Modi’s call to stop gold purchases
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: While welcoming Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call for prioritising locally-made products and reducing gold imports, the All India Gem & Jewellery Domestic Council (GJC) has said that India must balance “economic patriotism” and its cultural traditions when it comes to gold jewellery.

It argued that the sector contributes “nearly 7-8%” to the economy and supports “millions of livelihoods”. The GJC was reacting to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s recent and repeated appeal to all Indians to stop foreign trips and weddings, to buy local, and to only buy gold if necessary.

“The Prime Minister’s appeal for economic patriotism and greater preference for Swadeshi products is timely and welcome,” Rajesh Rokde, Chairman of the All India Gem & Jewellery Domestic Council (GJC) said.

“While we fully support the Prime Minister’s call for restraint when gold is viewed purely as bullion or an investment instrument, jewellery consumption remains closely linked to culture, craftsmanship, and livelihoods,” Mr. Rokde added.
He said that gold and jewellery hold a unique place in India’s cultural heritage, particularly during festive and wedding seasons, such as the period that India will soon enter in October-December.
“The jewellery industry, contributing nearly 7-8% to the economy and supporting millions of livelihoods, is an integral part of India’s growth story,” Mr. Rokde asserted.
‘People bought less gold, prices fell’: Modi recalls year-old appeal

“As a ₹10 lakh crore industry, the Indian jewellery sector must continue to grow responsibly, with greater transparency, value creation, and alignment with national priorities — balancing economic patriotism with India’s enduring cultural traditions,” he added.

articles.title: India, Finland seek to deepen economic ties through startup cooperation: Envoy Mikko Kivikoski
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: “India and Finland are looking to deepen economic cooperation by strengthening ties between their startup ecosystems and promoting greater two-way investment,” Finnish Ambassador to India Mikko Kivikoski has said.

"We want to engage more with the Indian startup actors. And of course, at the end of the day, this is all about advancing the economic cooperation between our countries. And here we see the startup sector, startup ecosystems, as an important part of that cooperation," Mr. Kivikoski told PTI .

The Ambassador was speaking at an unconventional startup event held at the Embassy of Finland in New Delhi on Friday (November 20, 2026), where entrepreneurs stepped into an ice-cold pool to pitch their ideas, drawing on Finland's winter-swimming tradition. "We have quite a long tradition in Finland for these kinds of events," Mr. Kivikoski said.

"This year has been record-high when it comes to interaction and engagement between Finland and India," he said, referring to visits by the Finnish Prime Minister and President, as well as meetings between the leaders of the two countries.

The Ambassador said the two sides agreed to elevate their bilateral relationship to a Strategic Partnership in Digitalisation and Sustainability during Finnish President Alexander Stubb's state visit to India in March.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi met his Finnish counterpart, Petteri Orpo, in New Delhi on the sidelines of the AI Impact Summit in February and in Oslo on the margins of the 3rd India-Nordic Summit in May.

Mr. Kivikoski also referred to the visits to Finland by India's External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal during the summer. "We see India as a trusted partner when it comes to the Indo-Pacific area," he said.
The Ambassador said the India-Finland relationship was increasingly moving beyond conventional trade towards a partnership involving investments and people-to-people exchanges.

"What we are seeing already, and what is happening between the European Union and India and between India and Finland, is that we are now talking about partnership. It's not anymore about me selling something to you and you selling something to me," he said.

"There are more and more Finnish companies coming to the Indian market and more and more Indian companies going to the Finnish market. And of course we hope, and we are confident, that this dynamism will continue in the future," he said.

Bilateral trade in goods and services between India and Finland stood at around $3.7 billion in 2025-26, marking a growth of about 25% over the previous year, and a 38.5% rise from $2.64 billion in 2021-22.
The startup event, Polar Bear Pitching, originated in Oulu, northern Finland, and has expanded internationally, connecting startups with investors and business networks.

articles.title: What does EPFO’s Systematic Withdrawal Plan entail for retirees | Explained
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The Story So Far: The Central Board of Trustees (CBT) of the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), in a meeting held in New Delhi on November 19, 2026 approved the Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) for EPF members, enabling periodic payouts of retirement savings. As per the proposed SWP, upon retirement or superannuation, a member will have several options to receive the accumulated PF corpus or a part through periodic withdrawals instead of a lump-sum withdrawal.

As of now, a retiring PF subscriber generally withdraws the entire provident fund accumulation as a lump sum. The proposal, cleared by the CBT, say an eligible member, upon retirement, may opt to receive their provident fund accumulations as monthly withdrawals; quarterly withdrawals; half-yearly withdrawals; or annual withdrawals. The remaining corpus will be invested within the EPF Fund and will continue to earn EPF interest on the running balance. The SWP scheme also proposes to provide flexible options to the member for enhancing his or her corpus in PF by voluntary contributions through payroll, direct additional contributions other than payroll and third-party micro-contributions.

articles.title: Infra push and low base effect pushes core sector growth to series-high of 10.9% in October 2026
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Growth in the core industrial sectors of the economy climbed to a series-high of 10.9% in October 2026, driven by a surge in electricity generation, and coal, cement, and iron ore production, and a low base effect, official data released on Friday (November 20, 2026) showed.

Data released by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on the Index of Core Industries shows that growth in October surpassed the 8.2% in September, the previous series high. The new index, released this year with a base year of 2022-23, has data that goes back only up to April 2024.
However, the data also shows that the strong growth figure in October was also likely aided by the fact that the index grew a relatively poor 0.8% in October last year.

“While core output surged by 10.9% in October 2026, the fastest pace in the new series, this was supported by a low base related to the shift in the festive calendar, with output having expanded by a marginal 0.8% in the year ago month,” Aditi Nayar, chief economist at ICRA said.

“While the growth print for October 2026 signals a strong start for the third quarter of FY2027, this is largely optical,” Ms. Nayar added. “The average performance for October-November 2026 would provide a better assessment, as this would adjust for festive base effects.”

Within the index, the coal sector saw growth accelerating to 23.05% in October 2026, far faster than the 10.7% registered in September. October’s performance, however, is likely also due to low base effect, since the sector contracted 8.4% in October last year.

The growth in the index, however, is in line with what the industry itself has reported. Coal India, the country’s largest coal company, reported that production increased about 19% to 67.2 million tonnes (MT) in October.

A major reason for the growth in coal production was likely demand from the power sector, which saw electricity generation jump by 21.6% in October 2026, up from 12.6% in the previous month. However, this sector too could have benefited from a low base effect, since it contracted nearly 7% in October 2025.
Within the index, the infrastructure-related sectors were the only ones that grew strongly without the aid of a statistical low base effect.

The iron ore sector, for example, grew at a three-month high of 23.4% in October 2026, compared to 18.4% in September and 8.7% in October last year. One of the factors driving this strong growth was that steel production grew at 7.3% in October, the fastest rate in seven months.
The cement sector also grew at a series-high of 15.4% in October 2026, compared to 10.1% in September, and 5.2% in October last year.
The fuel-related sectors in the Index other than coal continued to perform relatively poorly.

articles.title: Bangladesh vows to arrest ex-PM Hasina if she returns from India
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Bangladesh will arrest and jail former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina if she returns from India, a senior government Minister said, as her plans to come home in December 2026 fuel political tension and renewed street violence.

Dhaka is instead seeking Ms. Hasina’s extradition from India, where she has lived since fleeing Bangladesh in 2024, and expects New Delhi to comply with an existing extradition treaty, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam told Reuters.
India’s External Affairs Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In April 2026, the Ministry said it was examining Bangladesh’s request to extradite Ms. Hasina.
Ms. Hasina faces a death sentence in Bangladesh, and her Awami League party is banned following the 2024 uprising that ended her long rule.

The United Nations has said as many as 1,400 people were killed during the unrest. Ms. Hasina fled Dhaka in August 2024 as protests demanding her resignation swept the country. She has since sought a new passport and identity card ahead of a planned return in December, requests the government has rejected.

“As soon as she tries to enter Bangladesh, she will be arrested. And she will be taken to jail, and the law will take its course,” Ms. Obaed said in an interview on Sunday (November 22, 2026). “We would like India to honour the extradition treaty and return her as a convict, and the law will take its course. She (Ms. Hasina) will have to face the music.”

The standoff has brought Ms. Hasina’s Awami League supporters out on the streets. The party this month announced a week of protests and rallies in support of Ms. Hasina’s return, culminating in a nationwide lockdown on November 19, 2026.

Police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of arson targeting vehicles in at least 28 districts over the past 10 days, with several police officers and civilians injured, according to local media. Ms. Obaed called the violence a survival tactic by Ms. Hasina’s “politically bankrupt political party.”
Khalid Mahmud Chowdhury, a senior Awami League official, said the current political establishment was responsible for the violence.

The Minister said there had been no official discussions with India about sending an aircraft to bring Ms. Hasina back, adding that Dhaka wanted balanced ties with New Delhi that did not compromise Bangladesh’s “dignity, self-respect and interests.” “India needs to decide what kind of foreign policy they need to adopt for Bangladesh,” Ms. Obaed said.

Dhaka is also stepping up diplomatic pressure on neighbouring Myanmar over the return of Rohingya refugees, after the UN’s highest court ruled that thousands of killings and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar’s security forces against the Muslim minority in 2017 amounted to State-sponsored genocide.
Myanmar has criticised the ruling by the International Court of Justice and said Rohingya would only be able to return “when situations permit”.

articles.title: Nepal PM India visit LIVE: PM Modi announces offshore campus of IIT in Nepal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: “As a dependable and trusted neighbour, India consistently stood as the first responder in times of natural disasters and difficult times in Nepal,” Nepal PM Balen Shah said, adding that mutual respect, steadfast trust and unbroken goodwill are the bedrock of the relations.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while announcing the Development Cooperation Package of 24,000 crore Nepalese rupees, expressed his condolences over the loss of lives in the Nepal floods.

PM Modi announced that India will establish an offshore campus of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) in Nepal, alongside a startup incubator and an innovation hub, as part of a broader push to empower Nepali youth and deepen bilateral educational and technological cooperation.

“Friends, Nepal’s youth generation is full of talent, energy, and big dreams. India is fully committed to partnering in making their dreams a reality. To realise this resolve, we will establish a startup incubator, an innovation hub, and an offshore campus of the Indian Institute of Technology in Nepal,” PM Modi said.

Alongside setting up the IIT offshore campus, the Prime Minister announced expanded academic avenues in India for students from the Himalayan nation, stating, “We will expand scholarship opportunities in India for Nepali students in law and technology.”

Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a development package of 24,000 crore Nepalese rupees for Nepal after holding wide-ranging talks with his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah that produced many key outcomes to further solidify the bilateral ties.

Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah warmly welcomed Indian investors to Nepal and called for translating bilateral understandings and infrastructure milestones into tangible gains for farmers, youth, students, and entrepreneurs across both countries.

“We are clear that the outcomes of the understandings that we reached today, and the projects we advance, must translate into prosperity in the fields of our farmers, employment and opportunity in the hands of our youth, new horizons in the dreams of our students, and tangible avenues for new markets, investment, and business expansion for our entrepreneurs. I am confident that these historic milestones will elevate Nepal-India relations to new heights. The need of the hour is to stand on the sturdy foundation of this enduring bond,” he added.
India will establish an offshore campus of IIT, expand scholarship opportunities in Law and Technology for Nepali students in India, says PM Modi.
The Prime Minister underscored New Delhi’s role in keeping fuel, fertiliser, and other essentials flowing to Nepal under its “Neighbourhood First” approach despite supply pressures this year.

“In keeping with our ‘Neighbourhood First’ policy, despite severe challenges in oil supply this year, we maintained uninterrupted supplies of fuel, fertiliser, and other essential goods to Nepal. Today, the dedication of Phase II of the Motihari–Amlekhgunj pipeline and the foundation stone laying for the Jhapa petroleum terminal will further strengthen this partnership,” he stated.
The energy and fuel initiatives were unveiled alongside a Joint Vision Document aimed at advancing shared goals of “Viksit Bharat” and “Samunnat Nepal” he added.

articles.title: Israel at an Inflection Point
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Three years after Hamas’s October 7 attack shattered the core security promise of the state, Israel has emerged from a consequential Knesset election that ended Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing majority. Israel at an Inflection Point , published by The Hindu Group , examines how decades of unchecked militarism, a rightward political shift, and the collapse of the peace process have brought the country to this critical juncture.

The e-book brings together incisive essays by leading scholars and experts to offer a realistic picture of the strategic and political landscape surrounding the Jewish nation. Tracing the arc from late-19th-century European Zionism and the 1948 establishment of Israel to the geopolitical shocks of 2026, it probes the central tension between military dominance and durable security.

Across its chapters, the book explores how post-October 7 trauma has hardened Israeli opposition to Palestinian statehood, why tactical battlefield successes and high-profile assassinations have failed to produce a decisive strategic victory, and how rising American public scepticism and regional realignments are testing Washington’s traditionally unconditional backing. It also unpacks New Delhi’s pragmatic “de-hyphenation” policy, as India deepens defence and economic ties with Tel Aviv while maintaining its institutional support for a two-state solution.

For readers seeking a deeper grasp of a rapidly shifting West Asia, Israel at an Inflection Point provides essential historical depth and geopolitical context. Read this e-book to examine the domestic fault lines reshaping Israeli polity, the global economic fallout of the conflict with Iran, and India’s delicate diplomatic balancing act in the region.

· The evolving dynamics of the U.S.–Israel special partnership by M.H. Ilias

articles.title: U.S. panel urges India dialogue for Dalai Lama succession, warns of China legitimacy contest
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: A U.S. Congressional panel has recommended setting up a senior-level channel with India for succession contingency planning for the 14th Dalai Lama, contending that China may turn the process into an international contest over legitimacy.

A U.S. Congressional panel has recommended establishing a senior-level channel with India for succession contingency planning for the 14th Dalai Lama, arguing that China may turn the process into an international legitimacy contest.

The U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, in a report to the U.S. Congress, made a strong pitch to recognise the Gaden Phodrang Trust as the sole legitimate authority to identify and recognise the successor to the 14th Dalai Lama.
The report by the bipartisan Commission said China was likely to use coercive tools to shape the outcome of the succession process.
It said that the U.S. Congress should adopt a policy of not recognising any successor to the Dalai Lama who is selected or installed by China.

The Commission also wanted the U.S. to coordinate with allies and partners on a diplomatic response that denies international legitimacy to any successor selected by China.

It also wanted the U.S. to counter succession-related influence operations by strengthening the Central Tibetan Administration’s cybersecurity and resilience against China’s cyber and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled disinformation campaigns.

articles.title: COP31 talks fail as EU, others reject any climate deal without language on a fossil fuel phase-out
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: A standoff on a fossil fuel phase-out prevented countries at COP 31, the United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkiye, from achieving any consensus agreement on future climate action on Sunday (November 22, 2026), despite the conference running a record 48 hours into overtime.

The European Union led objections to COP 31 President Murat Kurum’s consensus cover text that failed to include any explicit language about moving away from fossil fuels. The EU’s stance was reportedly supported by about 130 countries.

On the other side of the divide, India is among the nations that supported the proposed cover text, as they want to keep using fossil fuels for the foreseeable future, with Environment Minister Bhupendra Yadav stressing that “climate ambition must go hand in hand with means of implementation.”

“We express profound disappointment with the final draft COP31 cover decision or Antalya Pact. At a point where the world urgently needs action to avert disastrous levels of global warming, the draft cover decision falls well short,” Ireland’s Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien said, speaking on behalf of the EU.

“We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5 degrees back to within reach… We will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel,” he added.

A cover text is an overarching political decision that frames the outcome of a climate conference rather than settling any single agenda item. It is usually finalised last, and like every outcome, it needs the consensus of all parties.

Panama also formally objected to the text, saying that as a country battling droughts and other perilous impacts of climate change, the lack of any commitment to keep the rise in temperatures below 1.5 degrees C with firm action on phasing out fossil fuels was “a setback”.

“Panama cannot support this decision. One, because it repeats previously agreed commitments without closing the gap between reality and what science demands. Two, because it weighs too much upon technologies such as CCUS [carbon capture utilisation and storage] instead of calling for deep changes, and three, because it weakens language agreed in previous decisions. This is a setback, a rollback,” said Ana Aguilar, Panama’s chief climate negotiator.

On the other side, Saudi Arabia, China, and India are among the countries that are against explicit language on fossil fuel and expressed comfort with the way the cover text language was framed, while also expressing misgivings about the lack of clarity on adaptation finance. The countries are part of the Like Minded Developing Countries (LMDC) coalition, who are insistent on the use of fossil fuel in the foreseeable future to further their economies, but have also significantly deployed renewable energy.

Indian Environment Minister Bhupendra Yadav said that India’s voice had shaped the draft COP 31 outcome, especially on food security, livelihoods, and cultural practices recognised in action on methane. However, in a post on X, he emphasised that “climate ambition must go hand in hand with means of implementation. Energy transitions must be nationally determined, just and equitable, backed by finance, technology and capacity-building for developing countries.”

Amandeep Garg, who was leading India’s delegation but speaking in his capacity as a spokesperson on behalf of the LMDC, said on the floor: “Everyone has worked tirelessly, and despite our discomfort with some elements of the text, we are willing to move forward, and continue to engage.” The LMDC expressed “concern” about the principles of equity and common but differentiated responsibility not being adequately reflected, adding that there was a “dilution” of the principle of developed countries taking historical responsibility and meeting their obligations.

“At the threshold of crossing 1.5 deg. C, we have raised a fundamental point – we need to reflect why we are here. Whose emissions, both past and continuing, have exhausted the global carbon budget? The cover decision does not reflect this, and only repeats agreed paragraphs from previous decisions to reflect responsibility and does not connect this with the imminent prospect of exceeding 1.5 deg. C,” he said.

articles.title: How did the COP31 climate agreement fall apart – and what happens now?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Two days after the COP31 global climate summit was supposed to finish, the talks in Antalya, Turkey, have come to an end – but not as we might have hoped.

Agreement simply could not be reached. The sticking point was the omission of fossil fuels in draft texts. The European Union led a revolt , shattering the consensus needed to adopt the cover text proposed by the Turkish and Australian conveners.

In a year of unprecedented climate disasters , a supercharged El Niño and as the world heads inevitably past 1.5 °C of warming , the EU and other nations said that the international process did not meet the moment .
Some coverage has suggested the rejection of the cover text is a sign the entire summit was a failure. This isn’t quite right.

These texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process. Countries have regularly agreed these political, overarching statements, particularly since the Glasgow meeting in 2021, but they are not a requirement.

Its failure does not signal the end of the COP process – or the breakdown of the Paris Agreement. What it may mean is that international climate cooperation will look different from this point onwards.

For many observers, the litmus test for success at COP31 was whether countries could make any headway on the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels. Unfortunately, fossil fuels proved unmentionable.

Three years ago at COP28 in Dubai, countries agreed to “ transition away from fossil fuels ”, marking the first time fossil fuels had explicitly been mentioned in an official decision text in decades of negotiations.
The Dubai text was hailed as “ the beginning of the end of the fossil fuel era ”. But there was little sign that hope would be realised in Turkey.

In a repeat of last year’s fraught negotiations at COP30 in Brazil, major fossil fuel producing nations Saudi Arabia and Russia banded together to block any reference in the negotiating outcomes and proposed cover text.
Australia and Turkey proposed a compromise – no fossil fuel language in exchange for support for electrification “with the greatest possible use of clean energy”.
This seemed to get Saudi Arabia over the line but drew backlash from the European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, and Belize, who rejected the cover text.

articles.title: How to tune into world radio music from a single app
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: If you listen to the radio while driving to work or doing the dishes, you’re probably familiar with five or so stations and regularly toggle between them in order to escape the ads. But imagine if you could point at almost any place on the map and tune into their radio offerings in real time. This is the premise of Radio Garden, which, in its own words, invites users to explore live radio around the world.

The process is simple: open the Radio Garden app or website to get to a Google Earth -like interface sprinkled with green dots, pick a radio station you’re interested in, and wait for it to load. If the station is available and responsive, you’ll soon be tuning into what locals are listening to.

Within a few minutes, a listener can explore futuristic Russian pop, soulful Palestinian songs, a French curation of classical pieces, or the sound of their mother tongue as they imagine millions of others going about their day.
A screengrab of the Radio Garden user interface on web | Photo Credit: Radio Garden

Radio Garden has something for listeners of every age. Users can explore multiple available stations from the same place, or tour different cities. The local time is shown for each location, helping you get a sense of the kind of music you might hear there.

The Google Earth-inspired interface is a fantastic way to introduce children to geography and the concept of time zones, as well as expose them to new cultures and languages through music . It can also aid in learning languages through immersion.

The listening experience on Radio Garden is always unexpected; we enjoyed Chinese traffic updates and Columbian tunes for a while and were later surprised to hear a Pakistani radio station playing a popular Bollywood song . A Cairo radio station gently awakened sleepy listeners at sunrise with soothing romantic songs, while one in Pyongyang at the same time kept up post-lunch morale with fast-paced group duets.

Radio Garden also offers curated playlists from stations all over the world for those who prefer a more thematic and cohesive listening experience, regardless of whether they lean more towards religious chants or rock songs.

Furthermore, a fun ‘balloon ride’ game in Radio Garden randomly drops the listener right into a new place and starts playing the local radio station. It then slowly increases the viewer’s altitude to reveal more of the map, even as one races to guess which country’s music they are listening to.

The free version of Radio Garden comes with full-page visual ads that can be closed after a few seconds. We did not encounter any audio-based ads that interrupted our listening sessions, which is a major plus.

Radio Garden has been operated by Jonathan Puckey as an independent company since 2019, per its website. The Amsterdam-based team founded the project in 2016 when it was commissioned for a radio-themed exhibit. The team worked to upgrade and maintain the experience throughout the COVID-1 9 years.

“ By bringing distant voices close, radio connects people and places. From its very beginning, radio signals have crossed borders. Radio makers and listeners have imagined both connecting with distant cultures, as well as re-connecting with people from ‘home’ from thousands of miles away,” noted Radio Garden on its website.

articles.title: How long is too long on the throne?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Every time I called my cousin Arun* around 9 a.m., his voice would echo, as though he were in a bathroom. “I’m on the throne, I’ll call you in 20 minutes,” he would say. The first time I heard this, it took me a while to understand what ‘the throne’ was, and as if that was not confusing enough, what was he doing there for 20 minutes. Perplexed, I asked him why he had the phone in the bathroom when he was doing his morning business, to which he casually replied that he would sit on the throne solving Wordle, crosswords and reading the news until he ‘downloaded’. A couple of months ago he told me that he was diagnosed with early stages of haemorrhoids and was on treatment. I advised him on this matter, stressing how his morning ritual could be contributing to his condition. This ultimately led to his ‘conscious reduction of phone time in the bathroom’. His words, not mine. Recently, he proudly announced that his scheduled ‘throne time’ was now down to six minutes, every morning after breakfast.

Bathroom humour is universal. Cinema is no exception — it has found humour and dependable plotlines from this predictable ritual. Just one instance is in Lokesh Kanagaraj’s Vikram , where a character pulling the flush coincides with the house exploding. Thankfully, the consequences of spending 20 minutes on the toilet are far less dramatic.

articles.title: In search of skin lightening creams, kidneys take a hit
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: On the heels of recent news reports on how keratin-based hair-straightening products containing glycolic acid derivatives led to severe kidney injury in women, researchers from Kerala have reported a series of cases wherein, the use of fairness creams has been linked to nephrotic syndrome.

In a study published in the latest issue of Kidney International (‘NELL-1 associated membranous nephropathy linked to skin fairness cream use — insights from an Indian case series’, ) doctors describe a series of 15 cases of Membranous Nephropathy, reported by Aster MIMS Hospital, Kottakkal, Malappuram district, that were traced to the regular use of fairness creams.

Heavy metal screening of the blood and urine samples of these patients revealed high levels of mercury, the toxic effects of which are well-known. An analysis of the fairness creams also showed that these contained high levels of mercury -- in some instances, 10,000 times above the permissible limit of 1 ppm.

Since 2021, Ranjith Narayanan, a nephrologist practising at two busy private hospitals in Kozhikode, had noticed a specific pattern in cases of membranous nephropathy diagnosed amongst his patients. They all had non-specific symptoms — fatigue, mild edema and frothy urine — but high levels of proteinuria, in the range of 6.5-22.2 g/day.

articles.title: Medicos warn against craze for fairness after 17-year-old Keralam girl diagnosed with kidney disorder
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The craze for fairness is more than skin-deep, and the trade-off can be costly. Inferior cosmetic products can end up harming your vital organs.

A 17-year-old girl in Keralam’s Malappuram developed a serious kidney ailment allegedly after using a fairness cream purchased online following its promotion by social media influencers, according to the doctors treating her.

The incident came to light after the authorities at the hospital that treated the teenager, who was diagnosed with membranous nephropathy, held a press conference on Friday. Lab tests had confirmed 1.25% mercury in the cosmetic product, according to the hospital sources.

Medical experts say that the use of fairness creams containing heavy metals such as mercury to lighten the skin is emerging as a major health hazard that can lead to serious conditions such as kidney failure if not diagnosed early.

Warning against following social media beauty trends and using topical creams seen online or bought over the counter without a prescription, M.M. Faizal, former president of the Indian Association of Dermatologists, Venereologists and Leprologists, says people lack awareness of how topical applications can enter the bloodstream.

“People are obsessed with fair skin. We have observed a rise in the number of people buying steroid creams that are easily available over the counter and applying them to their faces. Such steroid-based applications and creams containing heavy metals such as mercury can damage your kidneys easily. The government needs to bring in some mechanisms to control this,” he says.

A rise in the number of teenagers relying on spurious beauty products has forced the Keralam Drugs Control department to launch awareness campaigns targeting students in Classes XI and XII, an age group particularly vulnerable to online campaigns. Frequent inspections are carried out in marketplaces to confiscate spurious cosmetics.
State Drugs Controller K. Sujith Kumar says raising awareness about such spurious cosmetic products is the only way forward.
“We have seized cosmetics that have high mercury levels from offline markets. But there is no way to track or regulate online marketplaces,” he says.

Prolonged use of such creams can lead to kidney damage, says former secretary of the Nephrology Association of Kerala, Jayant Thomas Mathew, who has come across a few cases of kidney disorders among users. The condition could be detected early because the patients were aware of the symptoms.

articles.title: Core accountability: On core sector performance
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The core sector performance in October is a good example of how statistical distortions can create incorrect assessments of the economy. The 10.9% growth rate, a series high, has been celebrated as a sign of the Indian economy’s strength and resilience. There is, no doubt, an aspect of this has been reflected in the numbers, especially to do with infrastructure creation. However, the much more impactful factor behind the high core sector growth was a low base effect. The overall Index of Core Industries grew just 0.8% in October 2025 and so, in relation, the performance in October 2026 looked that much faster. This low base effect is even starker when looking at individual sectors within the index. The coal sector grew at a blistering 23% in October, more than twice its growth rate in the previous month. Yet, a large part of this was propelled by the fact that the sector had contracted nearly 8.5% last October. The rest of the sector’s growth was driven by demand of the electricity and iron ore sectors, or so the data show. The electricity sector also grew at a series high of nearly 22% in October, but on the back of a near-7% contraction in October last year. This base effect anomaly is likely down to the fact that the festive season starts at different but similar points every year. As such, a more accurate reading of the economy will be possible once the data for November are available.

The construction-related sectors seem to have seen genuine growth, a reflection of the government’s ongoing infrastructure push. The iron ore sector’s growth rate accelerated to a three-month high of 26.4% in October 2026 as compared to a growth of 8.7% in the same month last year. Steel grew at 7.3% versus 9.5% last year, and cement by 15.4% versus 5.2%. The economy’s dependence on government spending is not going to ease in the near future, and might even intensify as higher costs eat into companies’ profit margins. The core sector data once again highlighted a major reason for these higher costs — the oil and gas sectors. The crude oil sector shrank by 4.1%, its 22nd consecutive month of contraction. The natural gas sector, similarly, contracted 7.6%, a series-worst performance and the 28th straight month of contraction. A major reason behind high inflation in India is the underperformance of these two sectors and the resultant dependence on imported fuel. It is time the Petroleum Ministry candidly explains — to Parliament in December or to the public directly — why India’s fuel output has been continuously falling. If it is a matter of a lack of resources underground, that is one thing, but the underperformance of oil and gas public sector undertakings is quite another. Accountability needs to be set.

articles.title: Paper tiger: On the Green India Mission
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: That all was not well with the Green India Mission was clear even before its approval. After the UPA-I government announced it in 2008, the Ministry of Rural Development had objected to its financial design much before the Union Cabinet approved it in 2014. But the Environment Ministry proceeded anyway and retained largely the same arrangement when it revised the Mission in 2021. Following the Comptroller and Auditor General’s report, on November 19, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) upbraided the Ministry for the Mission’s virtual failure and for still not having issued the implementation guidelines for the revised form. The original 10-year vision was to expand forest and tree cover by 5 million hectares (mha), improve forest quality on another 5 mha, improve forest-related livelihoods for 3 million households, and sequester up to 60 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. The outlay was ₹46,000 crore. In 2014, the Cabinet approved ₹13,000 crore for 1.4 mha each of the first two objectives by 2018, but to be supported to the tune of 81.5% by Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA), National Afforestation Programme (NAP), and MGNREGS funds. In 2021-22, the Ministry folded the NAP into the Mission and, in mid-2025, unveiled a revised version with an allocation of ₹12,190 crore to improve forest cover on 25 mha by 2030, including 24 mha through other schemes. The government had thus expanded the primary target but left the Mission responsible for only 1 mha.

Together with the CAMPA, NAP, and MGNREGS funds never materialising, it is no surprise that the programmes to improve forest quality and forest cover have respectively fallen short by 91.8% and 97.5% vis-à-vis the 2014 target. The Environment Ministry had assembled a large programme around resources that it knew it could not control. Pro-climate work in practice ought to span government schemes to deliver action and justice, and the Ministry ought to have formalised the division of responsibilities and accounting system. The PAC’s new demand that the Ministry submit an implementation timetable is insufficient. From the Jal Shakti Abhiyan in 2019 to the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan in 2024, the government has often floated new programmes banking significantly on funds from existing schemes — an untenable policy when the latter also have their own obligations. And if the VB-G RAM G scheme was to also advance climate justice, the government should not have undermined the erstwhile demand-driven funding model and shifted more financial responsibility to the States. Climate action has to be timely, for which the Union government must dedicate adequate resources and proactively ensure that its initiatives are implemented.

articles.title: Going public on AI: On Anthropic IPO
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Initial Public Offering (IPO) of Anthropic , PBC is a mile marker in the arms race to develop superintelligent systems driven by generative AI . Traders valued the firm at $1.27 trillion, a denomination that is bound to become more and more familiar in an industry backed by an endless appetite for capital and unprecedented forms of financialisation. Anthropic’s statements emphasise warnings on the safety of its systems and the consequences of unbridled development of advanced systems. In the history of the development of this technology, this PR spin may just be a blip. After all, their testing has led to AI agents that have broken out of sandboxes and infected unsuspecting organisations’ internal systems: a deluge of agentic chaos that is already a reality has led to little signs of the firm backing its words with action. A familiar trend is playing out, with open source LLMs showing frontier capabilities that can back their erratic impulses, appearing in the space of just months, or sometimes weeks. Advocates of pacing the frontier and managing these emerging risks have been marginalised in a way that has little precedent in this century. It is time for governments to get involved, and specifically, for India to raise its voice on these risks, loudly and unequivocally.

While India’s AI industry is nascent, its positions on international forums carry the weight of a sixth of humanity. A mix of cynical calculations and practical considerations have blunted the use of that voice, for example in the U.S.’s hugely destabilising war of choice against Iran, and Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza. In taking a strong position on what could be the defining transformation of this decade, India has little to lose, and a lot to contribute. India’s AI policies are geared towards diffusion and research of helpful capabilities that can trickle down to the common citizen. The capabilities that the Union government and State governments seek to boost by leveraging AI are removed from the frontier research wreaking havoc within the information security profession around the world. Out-of-control AI agents promise, moreover, significant disruption to outdated government and private systems online. While India has little commercial leverage to curb San Francisco’s accelerationism, its voice is sure to be noticed. India’s focus on AI in international fora, such as the AI Impact Summit in Delhi, has been on consensus. This approach must change. India cannot be silent amid a U.S.-China technological race which could lead to catastrophic damage. New Delhi must not allow the U.S. to stop it from pushing for AI safety.

articles.title: Three to tango: On Trump, Xi, Putin trilateral summit
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The first trilateral summit between the Presidents of China, the U.S. and Russia , held in Shenzhen on November 19, reflected both the changing global order and the leaders’ shared desire to remain engaged with one another in an increasingly unpredictable world. For U.S. President Donald Trump, the summit was a platform where he could push for joint talks between the world’s three largest nuclear powers on reducing nuclear warheads. After the New START treaty between the U.S. and Russia expired in February 2026, Moscow had signalled that it was ready for talks, but Mr. Trump wanted to involve China as well. For President Xi Jinping, the summit reinforced China’s position as a peer competitor to the U.S. While Russia seeks to deepen partnership with China, the U.S. is looking to build strategic stability. And for Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom the West sought to isolate after he launched the invasion of Ukraine, the summit offered a seat at the high table. The decision to start trilateral talks on nuclear arms and the joint declaration, which stated that ‘a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought’, are steps in the right direction. But much will depend on what follows.

Many had compared the meet to the 1945 Yalta Conference, when Russian leader Joseph Stalin, U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill met to discuss the future of post-War Europe. But Shenzhen was not a summit of the victors of a major war. This was more about three great powers setting terms of engagement in a changing world. The summit failed to achieve any breakthrough on any of the issues on the agenda — nuclear arms reduction, non-proliferation or the Ukraine war — or even offer a road map for the future. Moreover, it is not clear if the Shenzhen spirit could be sustained in the medium to long-term as another President in the U.S. could take a very different approach towards Russia and China. The three leaders have called for reform of the UN. While it is a welcome move, any attempt to reform the international system and institutions must also involve other powers, particularly rising middle powers such as India, South Africa and Brazil. But the Shenzhen framework could bring greater stability and predictability to great-power relations. This is important given that two of the Big Three are currently waging two separate wars. The leaders should draw up a clear road map for nuclear talks and other key issues outlined in the Shenzhen declaration, with realistic and achievable objectives. Otherwise, the summit would amount to little more than another diplomatic photo-op.

This was more about three great powers setting terms of engagement in a changing world. The summit failed to achieve any breakthrough on any of the issues on the agenda — nuclear arms reduction, non-proliferation or the Ukraine war — or even offer a road map for the future. Moreover, it is not clear if the Shenzhen spirit could be sustained in the medium to long-term as another President in the U.S. could take a very different approach towards Russia and China. The three leaders have called for reform of the UN. While it is a welcome move, any attempt to reform the international system and institutions must also involve other powers, particularly rising middle powers such as India, South Africa and Brazil. But the Shenzhen framework could bring greater stability and predictability to great-power relations. This is important given that two of the Big Three are currently waging two separate wars. The leaders should draw up a clear road map for nuclear talks and other key issues outlined in the Shenzhen declaration, with realistic and achievable objectives. Otherwise, the summit would amount to little more than another diplomatic photo-op.

articles.title: Incomplete remedies: On Special Summary Revision of electoral rolls
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Following the Special Summary Revision (SSR) by the Election Commission of India (ECI) in some States that had undergone the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) , mostly in Phases 1 and 2, some 74 lakh names were added onto the electoral rolls. This meant that the electorate in those 13 States, that had shrunk from 49.61 crore to 45.22 crore after the SIR, has now gone up to 45.96 crore. The ECI has extended the SSR to States and UTs in Phase 3. As before, it requires no proof of citizenship or mapping to older rolls, and insists on personal notice before any deletion other than of the dead. It also directs Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) to cross-verify deletions personally wherever they exceed 2% of a polling station’s electors. Draft deletions in Phase 3 of the SIR averaged 17% , and reached 32.8% in Delhi . The ECI also offered another opportunity to electors deleted by the SIR in the seven States and UTs where it is still underway, such as Delhi and Maharashtra, to return to the rolls. Electors who did not return their forms can do so now, explaining the delay, and those who moved within the State can return through the enumeration form with proof of their new address. EROs will process these forms under Rule 21(1) of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, and restore the elector’s old EPIC number.

These “corrective” measures follow the Supreme Court’s observation on October 28 that forcing deleted electors to re-enrol through Form 6, meant for new voters, was an “error”. The ECI’s use of remedies that existed in the registration rules is a tacit admission that it went wrong during the SIR. But the measures are limited. They reach roughly 4.5 crore of the 13.37 crore struck off the draft rolls and do not cover electors who moved out of their States. Electors in States where the SIR has concluded, including Bihar and West Bengal, which have already voted on the SIR rolls, can return only through the SSR, by filing Form 6 as new voters, with fresh EPIC numbers and no record that they were ever on the roll. In essence, the structure of the SIR remains intact. Electors must still provide details from “the last SIR”, and those whose details are unavailable or do not match will be asked for documents in a manner that amounts to a citizenship test. The legality of the ludicrous “logical discrepancy” checks remains unaddressed. The 2002-03 special revision offered a better way. Those who had shifted homes were enumerated door to door at their new addresses. The Supreme Court must direct the ECI to return to that model.

articles.title: Talks without peace: On Russia, Ukraine, U.S. talks
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. earlier this month failed to produce a major breakthrough or bridge the wide gap between Kyiv and Moscow. Yet, they were a good beginning towards finding a political settlement to Europe’s longest war since the Second World War . In the two-day talks, hosted by the U.S., the warring sides agreed on some humanitarian measures, including prisoner exchange. U.S. representatives Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow after the talks to discuss the proposal. In the next stage, U.S., Ukrainian and European officials will meet in Berlin to discuss a coordinated European and Ukrainian position towards the peace process. As of now, Russian and Ukrainian positions remain far apart. Russia demands Ukraine withdraw from the territories of Donbas it still controls to stop attacks. Russia also wants to introduce limits to Ukrainian military capabilities and Kyiv to declare neutrality (give up its NATO ambitions). Ukraine, on the other hand, has rejected making any territorial concessions for a settlement and asked for security guarantees from the West so that Russia would not attack the country again.

That Ukraine survived Russia’s invasion and continued to resist Russian forces for almost five years is no small feat. But it has also paid a huge price for its resistance. The country has lost more than 20% of its territory. Millions have fled, while men of fighting age are being drafted into the military . Ukraine’s economy is kept afloat by European support, while its military continues to rely on NATO for weapons and other supplies. Until recently, the West stood united in its support for Ukraine against Russia, but that unity has since begun to fray. U.S. President Donald Trump, who has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel, is seeking to reset Washington’s ties with Moscow . European leaders, who initially sought to isolate Russia, have also started reestablishing contacts with the Kremlin. In October, Finnish and Norwegian leaders held direct talks with Mr. Putin. To be sure, Ukraine’s long-range strikes can hurt Russia, as the recent attack on the Kerch Bridge demonstrated. But such strikes are unlikely to change the Kremlin’s thinking about the war. As the conflict drags on, Ukraine’s position is weakening, and its allies are growing increasingly divided. After almost five years, Russia has failed to take a decisive victory. Ukraine does not have a credible path towards victory either. A diplomatic settlement, therefore, is the only way forward. The Abu Dhabi talks recognised this reality. But for the process to be meaningful, Europe must also be brought to the negotiating table.

fullParagraphs: A Delhi court on Monday (November 23, 2026) issued a non-bailable warrant (NBW) against YouTuber Dhruv Rathee in a 2018 defamation case.
Judicial Magistrate Anam Rais Khan issued the warrant in a case filed by Vikas Sanskrityayan alias Vikas Pandey over a video uploaded on Mr. Rathee's YouTube channel.
The matter has been posted for further proceedings on December 3. A detailed order is awaited.
Earlier on October 31, the court had issued fresh bailable warrants against Mr. Rathee.

On October 17, it had issued bailable warrants against him after a process server reported that his house was locked while attempting to serve notice. The court had also issued fresh summons to Mr. Rathee at his address in Gurugram, Haryana.
His advocate had submitted that Mr. Rathee ordinarily resides in Austria and had come to India for the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protests in Delhi.
The court had noted that Mr. Rathee was initially summoned in July 2019.
The case pertains to a defamation complaint filed by Mr. Pandey in 2018 after Mr. Rathee uploaded a video against him on his YouTube channel.

articles.title: ASEAN-India Maritime Conclave in Visakhapatnam calls for deeper cooperation to secure Indo-Pacific trade routes
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Policymakers, diplomats and naval officials called for deeper regional cooperation to safeguard Indo-Pacific trade routes, address geopolitical uncertainties and build a resilient blue economy as the two-day ASEAN-India Maritime Conclave commenced on Monday (November 23, 2026) in Visakhapatnam .

Organised by the India Foundation in partnership with the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), the conclave brought together Union Minister of State for External Affairs Pabitra Margherita, Andhra Pradesh Minister for Human Resources Development, IT and Electronics Nara Lokesh, Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Krishna Swaminathan, former Chief of the Naval Staff Admiral Dinesh Kumar Tripathi, India Foundation President Ram Madhav and ambassadors and strategic thinkers from ASEAN member states.

Addressing the inaugural session, Mr. Margherita said that ASEAN-India synergy was central to India’s Indo-Pacific vision and Act East Policy, adding that stronger maritime connectivity, disaster management and sustainable blue economy partnerships were vital as both sides marked the Year of ASEAN-India Maritime Cooperation.

Union Minister of State for External Affairs Pabitra Margherita (left), Vice Chief of the Naval Staff Vice Admiral Krishna Swaminathan (centre) and Andhra Pradesh Minister for Human Resources Development, IT and Electronics Nara Lokesh at the inaugural session of the two-day ASEAN-India Maritime Conclave in Visakhapatnam on Monday. | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

Admiral Swaminathan cautioned that geopolitical shifts, climate change, and extreme weather events were creating uncertainty across the Indo-Pacific’s 12 million square kilometres of exclusive economic zones, where security is tested daily by maritime terrorism, cyber threats, theft, and trespassing—challenges that require shared regional responsibility to ensure secure sea lanes.

Mr. Lokesh pitched Andhra Pradesh’s 1,053-km coastline—backed by four upcoming ports, a proposed ₹30,000-crore shipbuilding cluster at Dugarajapatnam, subsea cable landing infrastructure, and green ammonia exports—as an industrial and digital gateway for ASEAN supply chains.

Meanwhile, Mr. Madhav said that Visakhapatnam was among the country’s foremost maritime stations, adding that the conclave would deliberate on recent shipping disruptions and channel closures to revitalise Indo-Pacific commerce.

Over two days, delegates and maritime experts will discuss port modernisation, maritime domain awareness, coastal resilience and institutional frameworks to turn diplomatic convergence into regional partnerships.

articles.title: West Bengal to be renamed Paschim Banga
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: A proposal to rename West Bengal as ‘Paschim Banga’ will be tabled in the State Assembly on December 9, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said on Monday (November 23, 2026).

“West Bengal will be known as ‘Paschim Banga’ in English as well. The name must be written exactly as ‘Paschim Banga’. We will introduce a resolution in the Assembly on the 9th. After its passage, it will be sent to the Government of India for the necessary parliamentary and legal procedures,” Mr. Adhikari said after a Cabinet meeting at the State Secretariat.
The State is referred to as ‘Paschim Banga’ in Bengali, and the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government wants the same name to be used in English.
“The formation of West Bengal has a history dating back to June 20, 1947, and that history must be recognised. Instead of ‘West Bengal’, the name will be ‘Paschim Banga’,” the Chief Minister said.

The BJP leadership in West Bengal has often emphasised that the word ‘Paschim Banga’ is part of the history of the creation of the State, which bore the brunt of Partition, and that one part of it became East Bengal [ Purba Bangla ], which is now Bangladesh. By using ‘Paschim Banga’, the BJP wants to highlight how Shyama Prasad Mookerjee and others sought the State as a homeland for ‘Bengali Hindus’ during Partition.
On June 20, the BJP government observed Paschimbanga Divas, marking the date in 1947 when Jana Sangha founder Mookerjee moved a proposal in the Bengal Legislative Assembly to partition Bengal.

The Trinamool Congress government had passed a resolution to rename West Bengal as ‘Bangla’ in July 2018, but the Union government did not consider Mamata Banerjee’ government’s repeated requests to change the State’s official name to ‘Bangla’.
